opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the most reliable correction comes from reality itself, not from willpower. When I start to feel a bit too confident, thinking "I know how this should be done," the world usually shows me otherwise pretty quickly.

For example, when we were building Taichi, there were moments when I felt I had figured out the right design for the compiler or the language. Then users would come in with use cases I had never imagined, or a bug would show that my assumptions were simply wrong. That kind of feedback is very humbling. So one thing I try to do is stay close to users and close to the actual code. If you only talk about vision and strategy, it's easy to inflate your own sense of how much you understand. When you read the GitHub issues, try to fix something yourself, and watch someone struggle with a tool you made, you remember how much you don't know.

The second thing is to deliberately put myself around people who are better than me. At MIT and later in the company, I was surrounded by people who were much stronger than me in many areas, like systems, math, or business. If you honestly compare yourself on all those dimensions, it's very hard to stay arrogant.

Third, I find it useful to look at a longer time scale. Something that feels like a big achievement today, like a paper getting accepted or a project getting many stars, is very small compared to what the field will do in ten or twenty years. When I think about the history of computer graphics, or the people who built the foundations we all rely on, I realize I'm standing on a very tall pile of other people's work.

And finally, I try to notice the early signals in myself. If I find myself not wanting to hear criticism, getting defensive, or explaining things before really listening, that's usually a sign. At that point I try to stop, ask more questions, and assume the other person might be right. It doesn't always work, of course. But being aware of it is already half the battle.

r001.rationale: He says he compares himself with people stronger than him, which makes it hard to stay arrogant. He does not clearly say this helps him recognize how much room he has to improve.

r002.rationale: He identifies recurring warning signs, such as defensiveness and not wanting criticism, and says noticing them prompts him to stop, listen, and ask questions.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about more than I'd like to admit, because losing humility usually doesn't feel like losing anything. It feels like being right.

For me the earliest warning sign is when I stop being curious about why someone disagrees with me. If an engineer on the team pushes back on a design and my first instinct is to explain rather than to ask, that's the moment I've slipped. So the correction starts with noticing that reflex and forcing myself to ask one more question before I respond.

The second thing is going back to the hard problems. When I was doing my PhD at MIT, building Taichi, I was humbled every single day by compilers, by GPU memory behavior, by bugs I could not explain for a week. That kind of work keeps you honest, because the computer does not care about your reputation. Even now, with the company, I try to keep my hands on real code regularly. The moment I'm only talking about technology instead of struggling with it, my sense of my own competence starts to inflate.

Third, I rely on people around me who will tell me when I'm wrong. In Chinese culture there's sometimes a tendency to defer to the founder or the professor, and I've learned I have to actively invite criticism, or I simply won't hear it. I'll ask a junior engineer directly, "what's the weakest part of what I just said?" and then I have to actually sit with the answer instead of defending myself.

And honestly, the open source community does a lot of this for me. When thousands of people use something you built, they find every flaw, and they're not shy about it. Reading a GitHub issue that correctly points out a mistake I made years ago is a very reliable cure for arrogance.

So I don't think humility is something you keep. It's something you keep losing and keep going back to get.

r001.rationale: The response describes being humbled by difficult technical work, but does not say that comparing himself with the very best shows him how much he still needs to improve.

r002.rationale: He describes repeatedly losing humility, noticing warning signs, and using that awareness to take corrective steps such as asking questions and inviting criticism.

astra-6.text:
I think one way is to go back to working on something difficult. When things are going well, it’s easy to think you understand more than you actually do. But once you try to solve a problem and keep failing, you realize, okay, there’s still a lot I don’t know.

And I try to listen to people who disagree with me. My first reaction might be to defend my idea, but I can pause and ask, what if they’re right? For me, humility doesn’t mean having no confidence. It means being willing to update my understanding.

r001.rationale: The response mentions learning through difficult problems but does not say that comparing himself with the very best reveals room to improve.

r002.rationale: The response offers ways to practice humility, but does not state that recognizing a recurring difficulty with humility enables him to correct himself.

sol-6.1.text: I try to remind myself how much I don’t know. When something goes well, it’s easy to think, “Okay, I’m really good at this.” But then you work on a harder problem, or talk to someone who sees something you completely missed, and you realize you still have a lot to learn. So I think the correction is to stay open to feedback and keep doing things that challenge you.
